The required changes are now clear.

Remove the `useRulePipeline` conditional in `analyzer.ts` and always call `analyzeWithRules`. Keep the registry parameter optional to preserve the 74p work. In `fixer.ts`, remove the `useRulePipeline` branch and always use the rule path, deleting dead legacy code inside `processOneFile`.

Keep `analyzeParsedFile`, `fixParsedFile`, and `reorderFunctionDeclarations` in `analyzer.ts` for unit tests. Remove the dual-world gate from `tests/helpers.ts` so `fixCode` always uses the rule path. `analyzeCode` may optionally switch to `analyzeWithRules` for CLI-like consistency.

Update `rule-fix-coverage.test.ts` to reflect that no enabled rules still route through the rule path. Leave the legacy-versus-rule equivalence tests untouched. The analyzer does not need a registry parameter change.

In `fixer.ts`, `processOneFile` will parse the file, run `analyzeWithRules`, then conditionally apply `fixFileWithRules` when fixing. Legacy helpers such as `processAnalysisResult` and `fixFile` will remain only for direct test calls. The unused `analyzeParsedFile` import should also be removed from `fixer.ts`.

`processAnalysisResult` is dead code once the legacy branch is removed from `processOneFile`. `fixFile` remains exported for test usage. Whether `analyzeFiles` should accept an optional registry parameter is still under consideration.

`analyzeFiles` will not gain a registry parameter; the change stays minimal. `fixCode` in `helpers.ts` will always invoke `fixFileWithRules` directly, using `analyzeWithRules` afterward for equivalence checks.

`analyzeCode` should switch to `analyzeWithRules` for behavioral consistency. `fixCode` will call `getEnabled()`, so rules must be registered. `register-default-rules` is not imported by `helpers.ts`, unlike the CLI, which means default rules are not automatically available there.

Checking whether `register-default-rules.ts` is imported early enough to ensure default rules are active when `fixCode` switches to `getEnabled()`. Many fixer tests rely on `helpers.fixCode` without importing the registry module themselves, so the registration side effect must be guaranteed.

Since neither `analyzer.ts` nor `fixer.ts` imports `register-default-rules.ts`, `getEnabled()` would return empty when invoked from `helpers.ts` alone. The plan is to import the registry module in `analyzer.ts`, `fixer.ts`, or `helpers.ts` so the default rules register automatically.

Checking whether `cli.ts` imports `register-default-rules.ts` so the default rules register automatically for the library path. The module is designed for side-effect import, but `cli-runners` does not appear to import it.

import { fixFileWithRules, fixParsedFile } from './src/fixer';

console.log('---');
console.log('rule fixed', rule.fixed);
console.log('rule content:\\n', rule.fixedContent);

"
